summary: EPIRB, SART, survival craft VHF and NAVTEX: their jobs in a rescue, the numbers the exam asks for, and when to replace parts.

blocks.title: 4 radios, 1 rescue
items: EPIRB, Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon, 406 MHz: raises the alarm by satellite.
SART, Search And Rescue Radar Transponder, 9 GHz: shows the raft on rescuers' radar.
Survival craft VHF, channel 16, 156.8 MHz: survivors and rescuers talk.
NAVTEX, navigational telex, 518 kHz: prints safety warnings from shore stations on every bridge.

blocks.title: EPIRB
items: Hydrostatic release: a few meters underwater, pressure frees the beacon. It floats up and switches on.
Bracket magnet: prevents accidental operation while the beacon's secured.
Alert: short digital bursts, 5 W on 406.025 MHz, with the beacon's ID number.
Homing: 121.5 MHz, low power, for direction finders. Strobe light up close.

blocks.title: SART
items: Transponder: listens and answers. Switched on by hand in the survival craft, raised on its pole.
Standby: silent until an X-band (3 cm) radar pulse arrives: radar interrogation. Then it replies.

items.def: Local User Terminal, a ground station.
effective radiated power, what actually leaves the antenna.
weakest signal giving clear speech. Smaller number, more sensitive.

items.name: Distance between dots
items.means: A cycle is 7.5 + 0.4 = 7.9 µs. Radar mile: 12.34 µs per nm. Same at any range.

blocks.title: NAVTEX
items: Single letters identify stations (on a schedule) and categories: A navigational, B meteorological, D search and rescue.
Rejecting: choose a station's or category's letter (A to Z), then deselect it. A, B and D stay on.
Accuracy: each character is sent twice, about 280 ms apart. That's collective FEC, forward error correction: no ship can ask for a repeat.
No new messages, powers on, settings correct: a defective RF amplifier at the antenna base, powered through the coax.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: A 406 MHz EPIRB has no aural locator.
No 1-watt alert, no 121.5 MHz alerting beacon.
Not SART: 3 GHz S-band, dashes, spirals, 10 sweeps, 0.48 nm.
Channel 70 is DSC only, no voice, so simplex on it is false.
2187.5 kHz is MF DSC distress, not NAVTEX.
NAVTEX stations use letters, not two-digit IDs, SELCALL or 00.
Accuracy isn't a parity check or selective FEC.
